questionText: A relation R in a set A is called an empty relation if:
options: Every element of A is related to itself
No element of A is related to any element of A
Every element of A is related to every element of A
exactAnswer: No element of A is related to any element of A
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the definition of an empty relation in set theory.
Step 2: An empty relation means the relation set R contains no pairs, so R is the empty set (∅).
Step 3: Therefore, it is safely concluded that no element of A is related to any element of A.

questionText: A relation R in a set A is called a universal relation if:
options: No element of A is related to any element of A
Every element of A is related to every element of A
Only identical elements are related to each other
It has only one ordered pair
exactAnswer: Every element of A is related to every element of A
explanationSteps: Step 1: Recall the definition of a universal relation on a set.
Step 2: A universal relation contains all possible ordered pairs, meaning R = A × A.
Step 3: This safely means that every element of A is related to every element of A.

questionText: If R is a relation on set A, what condition makes it a strictly reflexive relation?
options: For every a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R
If (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R
If (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R
exactAnswer: For every a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the core mathematical property of a reflexive relation.
Step 2: A relation is reflexive if every single element in the set maps to itself.
Step 3: Mathematically, this securely translates to: For every a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R.

questionText: If R is a relation on set A, what condition makes it a strictly symmetric relation?
options: For every a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R
If (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R
If (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R
Every element connects to the origin
exactAnswer: If (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the core mathematical property of a symmetric relation.
Step 2: A relation is symmetric if every directional link works perfectly in reverse.
Step 3: This safely means that if (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) must also be in R.

questionText: If R is a relation on set A, what condition makes it a strictly transitive relation?
options: For every a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R
If (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R
If (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R
exactAnswer: If (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the core mathematical property of a transitive relation.
Step 2: Transitivity means if an element chains to a second, and the second chains to a third, the first must chain to the third.
Step 3: This is securely written as: If (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R.

questionText: What do we call a relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Review the classification of relations that meet all three core properties.
Step 2: A relation fulfilling reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity behaves like mathematical equality.
Step 3: Such a relation is safely and universally termed an Equivalence relation.

questionText: Let A = {1, 2}. Which of these relations is the identity relation on A?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the definition of an identity relation.
Step 2: An identity relation connects every element of a set exactly to itself, and to absolutely nothing else.
Step 3: For set A = {1, 2}, this safely generates the relation {(1, 1), (2, 2)}.

questionText: Let A = {1, 2}. Which of these relations is the universal relation on A?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the definition of a universal relation.
Step 2: A universal relation on set A includes all possible ordered pairs, meaning A × A.
Step 3: For A = {1, 2}, A × A safely evaluates to {(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)}.

questionText: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. What type of relation is R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)} on set A?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Test the relation R against the definitions of reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
Step 2: It lacks (1,1) so it is not reflexive. It lacks (1,1) despite (1,2) and (2,1), so it is not transitive. It contains (a,b) and its reverse (b,a).
Step 3: Since every pair has its reverse, the relation is safely classified as Symmetric.

questionText: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. What type of relation is R = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3)} on set A?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Test the relation R against the properties.
Step 2: It is not reflexive (missing 1,1). It is not symmetric (has 1,2 but no 2,1).
Step 3: It has (1,2) and (2,3), and it safely includes the required chain completion (1,3), making it Transitive.

questionText: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. What type of relation is R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)} on set A?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Analyze the properties of the relation R.
Step 2: It has (a,a) for all elements, so it is reflexive. If (a,b) is in R, (b,a) is in R (trivially true here). If (a,b) and (b,c) are in R, (a,c) is in R (trivially true).
Step 3: Since it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, it safely forms an Equivalence relation.

questionText: Let R be a relation on the set of real numbers defined by a ≤ b. What properties does this relation possess?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Check reflexivity: a ≤ a is always true. Check symmetry: if a ≤ b, it does not mean b ≤ a (e.g., 2 ≤ 3, but 3 ≰ 2).
Step 2: Check transitivity: if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then mathematically a ≤ c is always true.
Step 3: Therefore, the relation is safely concluded to be Reflexive and Transitive, but not symmetric.

questionText: Let R be a relation on the set of real numbers defined by a = b. What type of relation is this?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Evaluate a = b. It is reflexive because a = a.
Step 2: It is symmetric because if a = b, then b = a. It is transitive because if a = b and b = c, then a = c.
Step 3: Satisfying all three properties securely makes it an Equivalence relation.

questionText: Let R be the relation on a set of lines L defined by 'L1 is perpendicular to L2'. What type of relation is R?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Check reflexivity: A line cannot be perpendicular to itself, so it is not reflexive.
Step 2: Check symmetry: If L1 is perpendicular to L2, then L2 is definitely perpendicular to L1.
Step 3: Check transitivity: If L1 ⊥ L2 and L2 ⊥ L3, then L1 is parallel to L3, not perpendicular. Thus, it is safely Symmetric only.

questionText: Let R be the relation on a set of lines L defined by 'L1 is parallel to L2'. What type of relation is R?
explanationSteps: Step 1: A line is parallel to itself, so it is reflexive.
Step 2: If L1 is parallel to L2, L2 is parallel to L1, making it symmetric.
Step 3: If L1 || L2 and L2 || L3, then L1 || L3, making it transitive. It is safely an Equivalence relation.

questionText: Let set A have 2 elements and set B have 2 elements. How many total relations can be defined from A to B?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the formula for the total number of relations from a set with m elements to a set with n elements.
Step 2: The total number of relations is 2^(m × n). Here, m = 2 and n = 2.
Step 3: Calculating 2^(2 × 2) = 2^4 safely gives 16 total relations.

questionText: How many reflexive relations can be defined on a set containing exactly 2 elements?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the formula for the number of reflexive relations on a set with n elements, which is 2^(n(n-1)).
Step 2: Substitute n = 2 into the formula.
Step 3: Calculating 2^(2(2-1)) = 2^2 safely gives 4 reflexive relations.

questionText: A function f: A → B is called one-one if:
options: Every element in B has a pre-image in A
Distinct elements of A have distinct images in B
All elements of A map to the same element in B
The set A and set B have the same number of elements
exactAnswer: Distinct elements of A have distinct images in B
explanationSteps: Step 1: Review the definition of a one-one (injective) function.
Step 2: The defining characteristic is that no two elements in the domain map to the same element in the codomain.
Step 3: This securely means that distinct elements of A have distinct images in B.

questionText: A function f: A → B is called onto if:
options: Distinct elements of A have distinct images in B
Every element in B has a pre-image in A
Every element in A maps to itself
The domain and codomain are the same set
exactAnswer: Every element in B has a pre-image in A
explanationSteps: Step 1: Review the definition of an onto (surjective) function.
Step 2: A function is onto if the entire codomain is covered by the function's outputs.
Step 3: This safely means that every element in B has a corresponding pre-image in A.

questionText: A function that is both one-one and onto is mathematically called:
explanationSteps: Step 1: Recognize the dual requirement of a function being one-one and onto.
Step 2: A function hitting every target uniquely and leaving no targets empty is a perfect pairing.
Step 3: This perfect mapping is safely and formally called a Bijective function.

questionText: What is another mathematical name specifically for a one-one function?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the standard alternative terminology used in higher mathematics.
Step 2: One-one maps inject uniquely into the target set without overlap.
Step 3: Therefore, it is safely known as an Injective function.

questionText: What is another mathematical name specifically for an onto function?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the standard alternative terminology for mapping functions.
Step 2: Onto implies the function completely covers or surges over the target codomain.
Step 3: Therefore, it is safely known as a Surjective function.

questionText: Let the function f: R → R be defined by f(x) = 2x. What type of function is this?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Test for one-one: If 2x1 = 2x2, then x1 = x2. It is one-one.
Step 2: Test for onto: For any real y, there is a real x = y/2 such that f(y/2) = y. It is onto.
Step 3: Being both one-one and onto, it safely qualifies as a Bijective function.

questionText: Let the function f: R → R be defined by f(x) = x². What type of function is this?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Test for one-one: f(-2) = 4 and f(2) = 4. Since two inputs yield the same output, it is not one-one.
Step 2: Test for onto: The output is always non-negative. There is no real x for which x² = -5, so it is not onto.
Step 3: Therefore, it is safely concluded to be Neither one-one nor onto.

questionText: Let the function f: N → N (where N is Natural Numbers) be defined by f(x) = 2x. What type of function is this?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Test one-one: 2x1 = 2x2 implies x1 = x2, so it is one-one.
Step 2: Test onto: The codomain is N. Is there an x in N such that 2x = 3? No, x = 1.5 is not a natural number.
Step 3: Since it covers only even natural numbers, it is safely One-one but not onto.

questionText: Let the function f: Z → Z (where Z is Integers) be defined by f(x) = x + 1. What type of function is this?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Check one-one: x1 + 1 = x2 + 1 implies x1 = x2. It is one-one.
Step 2: Check onto: For every integer y, there is an integer x = y - 1 such that f(x) = y. It is onto.
Step 3: Satisfying both conditions safely makes it a Bijective function.

questionText: Let the function f: R → R be defined by f(x) = |x|. What type of function is this?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Test for one-one: |-3| = 3 and |3| = 3. Two inputs give the same output, so it is not one-one.
Step 2: Test for onto: The absolute value function only outputs non-negative numbers. It cannot output -2.
Step 3: Since it fails both tests, it is safely classified as Neither one-one nor onto.

questionText: Let R be a relation on the set of integers Z defined by R = {(x, y) : x - y is an integer}. What type of relation is R?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Reflexive: x - x = 0, which is an integer. Symmetric: If x - y is an integer, y - x is also an integer.
Step 2: Transitive: If x - y and y - z are integers, their sum (x - y) + (y - z) = x - z is also an integer.
Step 3: Since it holds all three properties, it is safely an Equivalence relation.

questionText: Let R be a relation on the set of integers Z defined by R = {(x, y) : x - y is an even integer}. What type of relation is R?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Reflexive: x - x = 0, which is even. Symmetric: If x - y = 2k, then y - x = -2k, which is also even.
Step 2: Transitive: If x - y = 2k and y - z = 2m, then x - z = 2(k+m), which is even.
Step 3: Proving all three properties safely categorizes it as an Equivalence relation.

questionText: Let A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(1, 1), (2, 2)}. Is this relation an equivalence relation on A?
explanationSteps: Step 1: An equivalence relation must be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
Step 2: For R to be reflexive on set A = {1, 2, 3}, it must contain (1,1), (2,2), and (3,3). It is missing (3,3).
Step 3: Since it is missing a required pair, it safely concludes as 'No, it is not reflexive'.

questionText: What must the range of a function f: A → B be equal to if f is an onto (surjective) function?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Analyze the definition of an onto function.
Step 2: An onto function requires every element in the codomain (Set B) to be mapped to by an element in the domain.
Step 3: This safely means the actual generated Range must completely equal the entire codomain, Set B.

questionText: If a function f: A → B is a one-one (injective) function, and set A contains 3 elements, what is the minimum number of elements set B must contain?
explanationSteps: Step 1: Identify the condition for a one-one function: every element in A must map to a unique, distinct element in B.
Step 2: Since set A has 3 distinct elements, they must map to at least 3 distinct elements in set B.
Step 3: Therefore, set B must safely contain a minimum of 3 elements.
